citations.text:
Setting up multifactor authentication for administrators using Operations Center
Procedure

Last Updated: 2026\-07\-31
You can set up multifactor authentication (MFA) on an administrator account by using the
Operations Center.

Before you begin
The following requirements must be met to set up multifactor authentication on an
administrator account:* The administrator must sign on using the Operations Center 8\.1\.2 or higher.
* The administrator account must be configured to use SSL sessions between the server and the
administrator.

Tip: Use the QUERY ADMIN command with the
MFAREQUIRED\=YES parameter to list administrators that are configured to use
MFA. Use the QUERY ADMIN command with the MFAREQUIRED\=NO
parameter to list administrators that are not configured to use MFA.

To set up multifactor authentication on an IBM
Storage Protect server administrator account by using the
Operations Center, complete the following steps:

1. Sign on to the IBM
Storage Protect server by using the
Operations Center and open the Command Builder window.
2. Specify the MFAREQUIRED parameter to YES by using
one of the following commands: 

	* REGISTER ADMIN: To enable MFA while registering an administrator account for
	the first time.
	* UPDATE ADMIN: To enable MFA on an existing administrator account.
3. To be successfully MFA enabled on the server administrator account, log out from the
Operations Center console and make sure to close the browser tab of the Operations Center
console.
4. Log in to the server by using the Operations Center, specifying the
administrative ID and password that is being configured. 
The Operations Center displays a QR code that encodes a shared secret that is generated
automatically by the server.

Remember: The same shared secret is required to enable MFA
on the spoke servers of the same administrator account.
5. Scan the QR code by using an RFC 6328 supported security application that generates a
time\-based one\-time password (TOTP) setup on the administrator's mobile device or workstation. 
Also, specify the following parameters, if required by the application: 

	* **Code Generation**: Time based
	* **Algorithm**: SHA1
	* **Period**: 30 seconds
	* **Digits**: 6

Note: The time that is displayed on the administrator's mobile device or workstation, where the
security application is installed, must be in synchronization with the server time.

Tip: Some of the supported security applications are as follows:
	* IBM® Verify
	* Duo Mobile
	* Google Authenticate
	* Microsoft Authenticator
6. Specify the TOTP passcode that is generated by the security application in the
passcode prompt in the Operations Center and select
Control to complete the MFA set up. 
If the MFA set up does not complete successfully, it might be because the TOTP passcode is
specified incorrectly. In this case, to set up MFA on an account, complete the following steps:
	1. Sign on to the IBM
	Storage Protect server again by using
	the Operations Center.The server generates a new QR code that encodes a new shared
	secret.
	2. Scan the new QR code by using the security application that is installed on your mobile device
	or workstation.
	3. Specify the new TOTP passcode that is generated by the security application in the
	passcode prompt in the Operations Center and select
	Continue to complete the MFA set up.
7. If the same administrator account has any spoke servers, then you must complete all the
steps provided in [Setting up multifactor authentication across a network of servers](/docs/en/SSEQVQ_8.2.2/srv.admin/t_managemfa_servers.html "You can set up multifactor authentication (MFA) across a network of servers to ensure an additional layer of protection for your account in the IBM Storage Protect server."). The administrator user on the spokes must
use the same shared secret that is generated in the [step 4](#task_s2f_5dm_rsb__step_dcc_rpz_xbc). The spoke servers for the same administrator account are not accessible until they
are synchronized.

Results
After the MFA is successfully set up for the administrator, the Operations Center does not
display the QR code, it displays a prompt for the TOTP passcode. For subsequent sessions, an
administrator must sign on with both the password and the TOTP passcode.

citations.title: Multi-factor authentication
citations.text:
Multi-factor authentication
Multi\-factor authentication

Last Updated: 2026\-09\-30
Starting with IBM® Storage Defender Sentinel 1\.1\.6, you can set up multifactor authentication (MFA) on IBM Storage Defender Sentinel new and existing user accounts. With multifactor authentication, the engine can act as an open authentication (OATH) server requiring users to authenticate the login process with a combination of the username, password, and a one\-time passcode (OTP). You will determine if you require this security feature and learn to implement it. Typically, an authentication app such as Google Authenticator is used to set up the MFA client\-side application. This functionality is disabled by default. 

If you decide to enable MFA on the engine, each user account will get an alphanumeric key to add in the selected authentication app. The user can use the 6\-digit OTP when logging into the IBM Storage Defender Sentinel user interface with their username and password.

* **[Enabling MFA for the admin account](/docs/en/SSR25EF_2.3.2/t_sentinel_enabling_mfa_admin.html)**  
You can enable time\-based one\-time (TOTP) multifactor authentication (MFA) on the IBM Storage Defender Sentinel `ADMIN` account.
* **[Additional MFA commands](/docs/en/SSR25EF_2.3.2/c_sentinel_additional_mfa_commands.html)**  
You can enable multifactor authentication (MFA) on IBM Storage Defender Sentinel individual user accounts. You can also generate QR codes for the users, and disable the MFA functionality.

citations.title: Multifactor authentication methods
citations.text:
Multifactor authentication methods

Multifactor authentication is a multi\-step login process that enhances security by
 requiring multiple verification methods, reducing the risk of account compromise from stolen
 credentials.

MFA requirements
RSC requires all local user accounts to use MFA. A 90\-day grace
 period for MFA enforcement begins from the time of first access.

RSC supports two primary MFA methods to verify user identity:
 Time\-based One\-time Password (TOTP), through an authenticator app, and
 phishing\-resistant passkeys.

TOTP through authenticator app
TOTP provides multi\-factor authentication for RSC. You use an authenticator app on a personal device, such as a
 smartphone, to generate a single\-use numeric code. RSC enforces MFA
 by requiring this code in addition to login credentials. This method works with any
 TOTP application that complies with RFC 6238\.

Passkeys for MFA
Passkeys are digital credentials that use public\-key cryptography for secure
 authentication. RSC supports web authentication through two types of
 passkeys: platform security keys stored on a user device and roaming security keys
 such as hardware tokens.

You can use passkeys in the following ways:

* Secure second factor: A passkey serves as an additional layer of security for
 MFA.
* Passwordless login: If an administrator enables passwordless
 login, users can authenticate using only a passkey.

Note: You can configure passkeys only after you set up TOTP for the user account. When
 you configure a passkey, RSC offers the passkey as the default
 authentication method at login. However, TOTP remains configured and available, and
 you can choose TOTP instead to login.

citations.title: Configuring MFA for your account
citations.text:
Configuring MFA for your account
Procedure

Increase the security of your account by enabling multifactor
 authentication.

Before you begin
Ensure that the following prerequisites are met:* Install an authenticator app on a mobile phone, computer, or other device.
* Verify that the authenticator app complies with RFC 6238 and provides a
 Time\-based One\-time Password (TOTP).

1. Log in to RSC.
2. Click ![Account](https://docs.rubrik.com/en-us/saas/images/ui-icons/User.svg) and select
 User Preferences.
The User Preferences page appears.
3. Click MFA \& Login.
4. Turn on Multifactor authentication.
The Configure MFA dialog box appears and provides a QR
 code.
5. Launch the authenticator app on your device and start the process of adding a
 new account in the app.
The app opens the camera on your device.
6. Focus the camera on the QR code.
If your device cannot scan a QR code, you can click Can't scan the QR code? to
 view a setup key for manually enrolling the account.
The authenticator app displays a time\-based one\-time password
 (TOTP).
7. In Verification code, enter the code displayed in the
 authenticator app to verify your mobile device.
8. Click Set Up.
9. **Optional:** 
Click Change Device.
Selecting this option updates or switches the device used for MFA.
10. **Optional:** 
Click Create passkey to create a passkey for web
 authentication.

Note: 

	* You can only create passkeys if your account administrator has
	 enabled the feature and you have configured TOTP.
	* Passkeys use biometric authenticators or security keys to protect
	 your account. You must only configure passkeys on trusted personal
	 or employer\-assigned devices.

The Create a Passkey dialog box appears.
11. In the Create a Passkey dialog box, ensure that you enable Use for
 passwordless login to configure a passwordless\-compatible
 passkey.

Note: The Use for passwordless login option enables
 authentication without a username and password. Disabling this toggle
 enables the passkey to function as a second factor for MFA. Some modern
 authenticators create passwordless\-compatible passkeys by default even if
 the toggle is turned off.

The Enter Passkey Name dialog box appears.
12. Enter a unique name for the passkey and click
 Done.

Note: RSC suggests a name in the `Type - Browser -
 OS` format. For example, `Platform_Chrome_MacOS`.
 The name must not exceed 255 alphanumeric or underscore characters.

A message appears that the passkey has been added to your
 account.

Results
You have successfully configured MFA for your account. RSC requires
 your credentials and a TOTP for subsequent logins. If you configured a passkey, you can
 authenticate with the passkey or TOTP during your next login.

Avamar supports RSA SecurID, which is a two-factor authentication technology that is used to protect network resources. You can use two-factor authentication (2FA) for FLR of guest virtual machine backups in the AUI. Avamar 19.7 and later releases support 2FA on AUI login as well.

citations.title: How user authentication and authorization work in NWUI
citations.text:
How user authentication and authorization work in NWUI
Multi-factor authentication for local users

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) adds an additional layer of security by using Time-based One-time Password (TOTP).

Administrators can choose to enable or disable MFA for a Local User in NWUI. A Local User cannot be configured with the Enable MFA option. To configure MFA:

1. Go to Authentication Server > Users .
2. Add a new user.
3. Select the Enable MFA option.

If MFA is enabled for a local user, perform the following steps to log in to the NWUI:

1. Go to the NWUI login page, type your credentials in the Username and Password fields, and click LOG IN .
2. If the credentials are correct, the TOTP Verification screen is displayed with a QR code and a setup key below QR code.
3. Use the Google Authenticator application on your phone to either scan the QR code or type the setup key.
4. You receive a six-digit code in the Google Authenticator application.
5. Type the six-digit code in the Verification Code field and click VALIDATE .
6. NOTE: Step 3 to 5 is a one-time process for a user. During subsequent logins, the user must enter only the six-digit verification code to validate. QR scanning is not required.
7. NOTE: The six-digit code that is generated in the Google Authenticator application refreshes after every 30 seconds. If the code refreshes, type the new code and click VALIDATE . Alternatively, you can generate the six-digit code by using the setup key.
8. NOTE: This feature is supported only in Google Authenticator application version 6.0 and above.

If you upgrade NetWorker from version 19.11 or 19.12 to version 19.13 or later, perform steps 1 to 5 for MFA-enabled local users created before the upgrade to enable login.

citations.title: Configure multi-factor authentication
citations.text:
Configure multi-factor authentication
Configure multi\-factor authentication

Multi\-factor authentication (MFA) adds an extra layer of security to the sign\-in process. When enabled, users must provide additional verification to access the platform.

Only the **Master Admin** role can enable MFA, and it is applied at the account level—meaning all users, including the Master Admin, will be required to use MFA once activated.

MFA can be configured using the following factors:

* **Trusted IPs**: Restricts user access to a defined set of IP addresses, ensuring that only sign\-ins from trusted locations are allowed.
* **Time\-based one\-time password (TOTP)**: Requires users to enter a code generated by an authenticator app during sign\-in.

For optimal security, we recommend enabling both Trusted IPs and TOTP.

**How MFA behaves with both factors enabled**
* **If only Trusted IPs are enabled:** Users can sign in only from within the trusted IP range.
* **If only TOTP is enabled:** Users must enter a code from their authenticator app to sign in.
* **If both Trusted IPs and TOTP are enabled:** Users must sign in from a trusted IP address *and* enter a code from their authenticator app.

**Configure MFA**
1\. In the lower\-left corner, select your account profile \> **Account info**.

2\. Go to **Security** \> **MFA**.

3\. Enable trusted IPs and/or TOTP. (See below for details.)

4\. Turn on the **Enable MFA** toggle.

5\. Enter your password and select **Confirm**.

6\. Select **Save**.

**Note:** To save certain settings, the Master Admin must enter the TOTP code if TOTP has been enabled.

citations.title: Set up TOTP authenticator for MFA
citations.text:
Set up TOTP authenticator for MFA
**Setting up TOTP**

If MFA is enabled for your account, you will be prompted to set up TOTP when you sign in to Keepit.

**To set up TOTP**
1\. Select which authenticator you would like to use. Then select **Start**.  

If you already have one, select **I already have an authenticator app** to skip the next step.

2\. Scan the QR code or search for the app in the App Store or Google Play. Tap **Next**. 

3\. Scan the QR code with the app and then enter the MFA code. Alternatively, tap **Text version QR code** to enter the code. 

4\. Enter the MFA code you see in the app and select **Confirm**.

5\. Multi\-factor authentication is on. Select **OK** to close. 

Now next time you sign in we'll ask for a verification code if only TOTP is enabled on your account or if we notice a login from an untrusted IP address.

**Resetting TOTP**
If you lost your device or have a new authenticator, you or your Master Admin can reset the TOTP.

citations.title: Backup security best practices
citations.text:
Best practices for backup data protection
Azure Backup security best practices to safeguard backup data > Pillar 1 \- Access Control > Multifactor authentication (MFA)

[Multifactor authentication (MFA)](/en-us/entra/identity/authentication/concept-mandatory-multifactor-authentication) adds an extra layer of security by requiring more verification during sign‑in. By enforcing a second factor, you reduce the risk of unauthorized access because attackers can't easily obtain or replicate this verification. MFA protects access to Azure Backup and backup data even when user credentials are compromised. Azure Backup supports securely managed, phishing‑resistant MFA to help safeguard user accounts. MFA is now enforced for all Azure portal sign‑ins and is extended to PowerShell, CLI, and infrastructure‑as‑code tools. To learn more, see:

* [Update on MFA requirements for Azure sign\-in \- Microsoft Community Hub](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/coreinfrastructureandsecurityblog/update-on-mfa-requirements-for-azure-sign-in/4177584).
* [Overview of MFA](/en-us/entra/identity/authentication/concept-mfa-howitworks).
* [How\-to enable MFA](/en-us/partner-center/security/mfa-for-users).

As a best practice, create two or more emergency access accounts. This action helps to mitigate the risk of being locked out of your Microsoft Entra organization when administrator sign\-in or account activation is unavailable. [Learn more about manage emergency access admin accounts](/en-us/entra/identity/role-based-access-control/security-emergency-access). Microsoft Entra ID also recommends best practices for all isolation configurations. [Learn more about Microsoft Entra ID best practices](/en-us/entra/architecture/secure-best-practices).

citations.title: How Barracuda Immutable Backups Can Protect You from Ransomware
citations.text:
How Barracuda Immutable Backups Can Protect You from Ransomware
Protecting Your Backup Data from Ransomware > Immutable Backup Protection

Barracuda Backup maintains immutable backup copies by preventing direct access to the data. BBS also offers protection against data modification or removal via API. This means that you can only access and remove data through the secure Barracuda Backup interface, which can also be secured using multi\-factor authentication (MFA). In addition, data stored in the Barracuda Cloud is written once and never updated, providing an additional layer of protection. 

Secure Cloud Storage (Air Gap)
Data stored in the Barracuda Cloud is encrypted and can only be accessed, modified, or deleted through the secure Barracuda Backup interface. There is also a delay in the purging of data in the cloud so that data can still be recovered if it is accidentally or maliciously deleted from the local appliance. This creates an air gap between the appliance and the cloud, further protecting data against ransomware.

Multi\-Factor Authentication (MFA)
Multi\-Factor Authentication (MFA) provides an additional layer of security to the accounts and credentials used to access Barracuda Backup. With MFA, the attackers not only need the login and password, but they also need a secondary device and application to confirm the identity of the backup administrator.

Hardened Linux Platform
Barracuda Backup runs on a hardened Linux platform, which makes it less susceptible to malware and ransomware attacks compared to other similar Windows\-based backup solutions. The platform also prevents any unauthorized services from running, thus preventing the execution and spread of ransomware throughout the backup data.

Integrated Backup Software, Storage, and Offsite Storage
An integrated backup appliance eliminates any network sharing protocols and reduces the risk of the backup storage being attacked. Having an integrated solution that includes the backup software, storage, and offsite storage also reduces the number of attack surfaces making it easier to secure the entire solution.

Role\-Based Access Control
Following the principle of least privilege, users accessing the backup system should only be given privileges which are essential to their specific role. With Barracuda Backup, you can assign various user roles from full account administrators to restricted users and users with view\-only permissions. This minimizes the chances that an attacker can access the backup system with the most powerful administrative privileges.

No Network Sharing Protocols
It is common to store backups on Network Attached Storage (NAS) devices using a network sharing protocol, such as Network File System (NFS) or Common Internet File System (CIFS). An attacker can easily discover and access these file shares, putting backup data at risk. Barracuda Backup does not expose any network file sharing protocols, thus preventing access to the backup storage.

End\-to\-End Encryption
Barracuda Backup provides AES 256\-bit encryption of data at rest on the appliance, in transit whenever it is sent offsite, and stored at rest on the replication destination. All communication with the appliance is also done over an encrypted VPN tunnel. Encryption renders the backup data unreadable to an attacker who has gained access to it.

Restricted IP/Network Access
You can set IP login restrictions for each user who has access to Barracuda Backup. Those restrictions prevent access to the web interface from an IP address outside of the specified range.

Multiple Backup Copies
Barracuda Backup strongly recommends that you follow the 3\-2\-1 rule to create a successful data protection and disaster recovery plan:

* **3** –You must have at least 3 copies of your data: the original production data and 2 backup copies.
* **2** – You must use at least 2 different types of media to store the copies of your data. For example, the local Barracuda Backup device and Barracuda Cloud storage.
* **1** – You must keep at least 1 backup offsite. For example, in the Barracuda Cloud or on another physical or virtual Barracuda Backup appliance at a remote site.

In addition to the plan above, Barracuda Networks also delays the purging of backup data stored in the Barracuda Cloud, which provides an extra layer of protection in case of an attack or accidental deletion of data.

Two\-factor authentication in software has become a requirement in today’s cyberthreat landscape. Barracuda strongly recommends using two\-factor authentication, configured in conjunction with Barracuda Cloud Control.

Two-Factor Authentication

Two\-factor authentication prevents an unauthorized person from accessing your CommCell account.

* Command line

question: Which backup products can scan backups for signs of ransomware, such as unusual changes or encryption, and alert on them?
answer:
Commvault (Commvault Cloud): Commvault Threat Scan uses a machine learning-based encryption model to detect ransomware-driven or unauthorized encryption in backup files by analyzing structure and statistical properties such as high entropy, and monitors the environment for ransomware indicators like unusual file changes and anomalies [1][2][3].
Druva (Druva): Ransomware Detection uses a multi-stage framework with ML models to analyze backup snapshots for high-risk indicators (mass renaming, ransom notes, suspicious extensions), then performs forensic validation to confirm encryption and sends email alerts [4][5].
IBM (Storage Defender, Storage Protect): Storage Defender Data Protect uses behavioral anomaly detection and ML to monitor data ingest patterns during backups and alert on unusual spikes indicating possible ransomware [6][8]; Storage Protect's Operations Center examines backup statistics such as workload increases and deduplication rate decreases for signs of ransomware infection and issues security notifications [7].
Cohesity (DataProtect, FortKnox, Security Center): Ransomware detection in Cohesity Data Cloud uses ML and statistical anomaly detection to monitor changes in data volume, entropy, and file system changes across snapshots [9]; FortKnox checks protection runs for anomalies and sends email alerts based on a configurable anomaly strength threshold [10]; Enhanced Anomaly Detection analyzes entropy of backed-up file content to identify encryption earlier [11].
Veeam (Veeam Backup & Replication): Inline Scan uses inline entropy analysis during backup jobs to detect malware-encrypted files, onion addresses, and ransom notes, creating malware detection events, complemented by file system activity analysis, signature-based detection, YARA, and third-party antivirus scanning [12][13].
AvePoint (Cloud Backup for Salesforce, Cloud Backup for Google Workspace, Cloud Backup for Microsoft 365): The Unusual Activities Analysis report learns backup activity patterns and warns of organizations, drives, or sites with unusual activities or under potential ransomware attack, with email notifications [14][15][16].
Datto (BCDR): Ransomware Detection detects patterns of change in specific file types (e.g., in-place overwrites with random data, preserved timestamps) and alerts on suspected ransomware infections during backups [17][18].
Eon (Eon): Eon examines structured database data elements (row/table count drops, schema changes, cardinality shifts, corruption patterns, embedded ransom notes) for ransomware indicators, correlates signals into a weighted confidence score, and provides ransomware notifications [19][20].
Microsoft (Azure Backup): Azure Backup integrates with Microsoft Defender for Cloud to detect compromise indicators such as disruption patterns, behavioral anomalies, and ransomware signatures, and evaluates restore point health, with integration to preserve recovery points on ransomware alerts [21][22].
Dell (PowerProtect Data Manager): Anomaly Detection alerts indicate anomalies in backup copies, including direct matches to well-known ransomware, with severity based on extension risk and options to mark copies as Verified Safe or Quarantined [23][24].
Keepit (Keepit): Anomaly Detection continuously monitors backup snapshots and compares each new snapshot against the previous 60 snapshots, flagging significant deviations in the volume of changes as anomalies that can indicate ransomware [25].
Rubrik (Rubrik Security Cloud): Anomaly Detection in Data Threat Analytics scans snapshot data to detect ransomware attacks, VM Encryption Detection flags ransomware targeting ESXi hosts by scanning backup event errors, and Data impact investigation scopes affected objects and files for recovery [27][28].
Acronis (Cyber Protect Cloud, Cyber Protect On-premises): Backup scanning plans automatically scan selected backup archives for malware including ransomware once an hour via a cloud agent [29][30].
Bacula (Bacula): A security plugin provides backup poisoning detection by marking jobs with unexpected values in the amount of data processed, which could result from ransomware activity, and reports jobs where viruses or malware are found [31].
AWS (AWS Backup): AWS Backup integrates with Amazon GuardDuty Malware Protection to automatically scan backups after backup completion or via on-demand scans, detecting malicious code and identifying clean recovery points [33][34].
Trilio (Trilio for Kubernetes): Trilio's ransomware protection includes Detect and Mitigate capabilities such as scanning of backups/snapshots, anomaly detection, and notifications into Slack/Teams [35].
Zerto (Zerto): Encryption Detection uses real-time inspection of protected VM writes to identify anomalous encryption activity, issues the ENC0001 alert, and automatically tags checkpoints in the Zerto journal [39][40].
HYCU (R-Cloud Hybrid Cloud Edition): R-Shield policies provide anomaly detection of backup data size changes and malware scanning of backed-up data using YARA rules, with statuses visible per restore point [43][44].
Arcserve (Arcserve UDP): The Assured Security - Malware Scan scans backup or copy data in recovery points for malware or malicious files and warns about malicious files before restoring [45].
Arctera (Backup Exec): The Malware Detection feature scans VMware and Hyper-V virtual machine backup sets using Windows Defender or Symantec Protection Engine, ad hoc or as part of restore, and reports malware scan status [47].
Atempo (Lina, Tina): Atempo detects unusual or suspicious backup activity on agents, such as unusual amounts of protected volume sent or sudden changes in an agent's compression rate (for example, in a cryptovirus attack), and triggers alerts [49].
Unitrends (Unitrends Unified Backup): The Backup History report includes an At Risk field indicating whether a potential ransomware infection was discovered in a backup [55].
Afi.ai (Afi.ai): The Afi platform includes a ransomware detection module as part of its security and audit reporting and notification mechanism [57].
No supporting passage found for: Axcient, Barracuda, CloudAlly, CloudCasa, Flosum, GRAX, Gearset, Google, Hornetsecurity (Altaro), N-Able, Nakivo, NinjaOne (Dropsuite), Portworx, Red Hat, Salesforce, Slide, Spanning, Storware, Synology, Velero.

citations.title: Threats
citations.text:
Threats
Monitoring Threats > Encryption Detection

**Encryption Detection** identifies ransomware\-driven or unauthorized file encryption activity within backup files. 

Commvault Threat Scan employs a machine learning based encryption model trained to distinguish normal file content from encrypted data, providing greater accuracy, fewer false positives, and faster scan performance. 

The detection process analyzes the structure and statistical properties of file data to identify encryption\-like characteristics such as high entropy, data randomness, and irregular compression signatures while avoiding dependency on prior backup comparisons. This enables precise detection of ransomware\-encrypted content and accelerates identification of the last known clean restore point, ensuring rapid and reliable recovery. 

Detection Logic
* Telemetry Source: AI\-based model trained on encrypted and non\-encrypted datasets
* Operation: Detected during scheduled scans, restore scans, Cleanroom Threat Scans, and Threat Hunting (when encryption detection is enabled)
* Trigger Condition: Triggered when backup content exhibits encryption\-like properties or file entropy indicative of ransomware encryption patterns

Configuration
To enable Encryption Detection, the resource must be assigned to a Threat Scan plan. The Threat Scan plan automatically configures indexing and anomaly detection for supported workloads. 

Supported Workloads
* Windows file system resources (Indexing Version 2\)
* Linux file system resources (Indexing Version 2\)
* Virtual Machines (Indexing Version 2\)
* Network shares (Indexing Version 2\)
* Cloud file objects

citations.title: Monitoring Sensitive Data and Anomalies
citations.text:
Monitoring Sensitive Data and Anomalies

Because there is the potential for ransomware to infect computers and files in your backup environment, Commvault monitors and analyzes your environment to identify the possible presence of ransomware on your infrastructure computers. 

Unusual changes in files, backup files, emails, or file types may indicate that your backup environment has been infected, corrupted, changed, or encrypted, or may contain indicators of other means of compromise. These types of threats can impact recovery objectives if your recovery process is prolonged due to manual validation processes. 

Insights into file changes or anomalies allow you to respond effectively with preventative and corrective actions, such as:

* Isolated recoveries of backups for forensic investigation
* Automatic recoveries of last known good versions of data
* Deep level entropy analysis of backup content
* Scanning of data backups for ransomware

citations.title: Get Started with Ransomware Detection
citations.text:
Get Started with Ransomware Detection
**How it Works: The Multi\-Stage Framework** > **Stage 1: Potential Ransomware Detection of Ransomware Activity**

During this stage, Druva uses proprietary enhanced Machine Learning (ML) models to continuously analyze backup snapshots for high\-risk behavioral indicators, including mass renaming, ransom notes, and suspicious file extensions. If any high\-risk indicators are detected, Druva generates a “Suspicious Indicators Found” notification via [email](https://help.druva.com/en/articles/8513163-configure-alert-settings-for-cyber-resiliency) to alert you to potential ransomware activity, automatically escalating the affected snapshot for forensic analysis.

**Stage 2: Forensic Validation of Ransomware Activity**
When Stage 1 flags a snapshot for potential ransomware activity, the system automatically initiates Stage 2 to conduct an in\-depth forensic analysis and confirm active encryption. To ensure high accuracy, this confirmation relies on a robust, multi\-layered process that evaluates multiple indicators of encryption and file tampering rather than a single signal. Once confirmed, an **Encryption Detected** alert is sent via [email](https://help.druva.com/en/articles/8513163-configure-alert-settings-for-cyber-resiliency) alongside supporting evidence to enable confident incident response.

citations.title: FAQ's for Ransomware Detection
citations.text:
FAQ's for Ransomware Detection

📝**NOTE**: The availability of this feature may be limited based on the license type, region, and other criteria. To enable this feature, contact support.

What is Ransomware Detection?
**Ransomware Detection** is a multi\-stage detection framework that utilizes Machine Learning (ML) and pattern recognition to identify ransomware activity within backed up data. It analyzes key ransomware indicators and behavioral patterns such as suspicious file extension changes, dropped artifacts, and encryption techniques to generate high\-confidence, explainable alerts. This enables precise differentiation between legitimate operational activity and malicious behavior.

How is Ransomware Detection different from Data Anomalies?
Ransomware Detection and Data Anomalies serve different purposes. Ransomware Detection confirms ransomware impact with evidence. Data Anomalies flags deviations from baseline activity that may or may not be malicious.

| **Criteria** | **Ransomware Detection** | **Data Anomalies** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Purpose | Confirm ransomware impact | Flag unusual data activity |
| Detection method | Behavioral correlations \& Forensic Validations | Anomaly\-based |
| Zero\-day coverage | Yes | No |
| False positives | Minimal | Low |

How is Ransomware Detection different from Threat Watch?
Threat Watch detects known malicious files using IOC (Indicator of Compromise) signatures. Ransomware Detection uses behavioral analysis to identify ransomware activity. This includes unknown and zero\-day variants that Threat Watch cannot detect.

| **Criteria** | **Ransomware Detection** | **Threat Watch** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Detection method | Behavioral based correlations | IOC/signature\-based |
| Zero\-day coverage | Yes | No |
| Known threat detection | Yes | Yes (very high accuracy) |
| False positives | Minimal | Minimal |

How frequently does Ransomware Detection run?
Ransomware Detection runs at an interval of every 6 hours.

What workloads are supported for Ransomware Detection?
Here’s the list:

* VMware VMs
* Azure VMs
* AWS EC2
* AWS EBS

What happens to Encryption alerts generated by Data Anomaly?
If you have both Data Anomaly and Ransomware Detection enabled, the encryption check via Ransomware Detection takes precedence.

Can Ransomware Detection identify the ransomware family?
Ransomware Detection can identify known ransomware families when disallowed extensions or known ransom note patterns are detected. For unknown variants, the system identifies the attack based on behavioral patterns. It does not attribute unknown variants to a specific family.

What if Ransomware Detection generates a false positive?
If you believe a snapshot was incorrectly flagged, follow these steps:

1. Review the detection evidence in the alert details.
2. If you confirm the snapshot is clean, use the **Mark as not impacted** option to release it from quarantine.

Does Ransomware Detection require additional licensing?
Yes, Ransomware Detection requires the Premium Security SKU.

How does quarantine work?
When Ransomware Detection confirms ransomware impact, you must isolate the infected resource to prevent further spread of infection. Quarantined snapshots cannot be restored until you release them. This prevents accidental restoration from infected backups.

citations.text:
Detecting ransomware attacks

Last Updated: 2026\-03\-23

Ransomware can take over enterprise data and threaten to publish it or block access to it until a
ransom is paid. Backups, once considered defense against ransomware, are now a prime target for
ransomware that destroys shadow data copies and restore point data.

IBM® Storage Defender® Data Management Service uses machine learning algorithms to
continuously monitor changes in the backup data ingestion rate for your organization. If the rate is
out of the normal range—based on daily and historical rates—Data Management flags it as a potential ransomware attack and
alerts both your IT administrators and the Data Management platform support team. Administrators can then perform rapid restores from the last healthy
snapshot to recover VMs, files, and application objects.

citations.title: Security
citations.text:
Security
Monitoring security notifications > About this task

Monitoring security notifications
Last Updated: 2026\-07\-31
The Operations Center examines backup data for
clients for signs of ransomware infection. Respond to these notifications to determine if atypical
backup statistics were the result of significant but known changes in the backup data, or the result
of a ransomware attack.

Ransomware is a serious security threat that can result in data loss and render systems unusable.
Because a ransomware attack typically creates encrypted copies of many client files, certain changes
in backup data might indicate that a client is infected. When the security notifications feature is
enabled, the Operations Center can help you detect possible
ransomware attacks. The Operations Center looks for signs of
ransomware infection by examining backup statistics for indicative changes to the backup workload
and data deduplication rate. A significant increase in the workload might indicate that ransomware
encrypted many files on the client. A significant decrease in deduplication savings might indicate a
ransomware attack because encrypted files are not deduplicated. 

A security notification can show only that significant changes in the workload or data
deduplication rate were observed in the most recent client backup session as compared to recent
history. The Operations Center cannot determine the causes of
significant changes in the backup data, so a security notification does not necessarily mean that
the client is infected. The client might be backing up more data, or backing up more data that is
unsuited for data deduplication, for harmless reasons. For example, the client might be backing up
many new files because it recently mounted a new file system. Or the client might have encrypted
files, making them unsuitable for deduplication.

IBM® Storage Protect examines backup
session data for backup\-archive clients and for IBM Storage Protect for Virtual Environments clients. Security notifications are issued in
the Operations Center so that you can investigate further, and
determine why the statistical anomaly occurred. Open the Security Notifications
page to view the notifications by client, and examine notification details. 

Procedure
To open the Security Notifications page, on the Operations Center menu bar, click Overviews \> Security.

citations.title: Cohesity Security Features
citations.text:
Cohesity Security Features
Detect Anomalies

You can connect your Cohesity cluster to Cohesity Data Cloud and keep track of anomalous snapshots in your cluster. Ransomware detection in Helios is based on machine learning and statistical anomaly detection techniques to identify sudden changes in the data across snapshots over time. When these changes are detected, it might be indicative of ransomware compromising the data.

Cohesity Data Cloud constantly monitors the metrics, such as how many modified snapshots, and detects any anomalies. In addition, it uses machine learning algorithms to monitor change rates in the backup data continuously.

Cohesity's ransomware detection techniques can analyze changes in:

1. The volume of data read or written over time - noticing whether the volume of data protected from one protection job run to the next changed dramatically.
2. Analyzing changes in data entropy - very good for detecting when the contents of files may have changed dramatically due to encryption or compression
3. Changes in the nature of the file system - identifying when a large number of files has been added, deleted, or modified

If the rate is out of the normal range - based on daily and historical rates - Cohesity flags it as a potential ransomware attack. Refer to Detect Ransomware Attacks to learn more about how Cohesity Data Cloud detects anomalies.

citations.title: Enhanced Anomaly Detection
citations.text:
Enhanced Anomaly Detection
Enhanced Anomaly Detection

Enhanced Anomaly Detection (Entropy-Based) strengthens Cohesity ransomware detection by analyzing the content randomness of backed-up files, in addition to the metadata signals used by standard anomaly detection. By inspecting the actual file data rather than relying only on aggregate backup statistics, Enhanced Anomaly Detection identifies encryption activity earlier and with higher confidence. On the Anomaly Detection page and in the object details, entropy-based findings appear in the Assessment column with an explanation of the detection.

Note: This is a Private Preview feature. Contact your Cohesity account team to enable the feature.

A tooltip highlights an entropy analysis indicating two ransomware indicators: 569 files with known ransomware extensions and 509 files appearing encrypted.

citations.title: Inline Scan
citations.text:
Inline Scan

To scan blocks in a data stream, Veeam Backup \& Replication uses inline entropy analysis. During the backup job, the following malware activity can be detected:

* Files encrypted by malware. A malware detection event will be created if the amount of encrypted data exceeds scan sensitivity limits.
* Text artifacts created by malware:

* V3 onion addresses that consist of 56 symbols in the \[a\-z2\-7]{56}.onion format. For example, vykenniek4sagugiayj3z32rpyrinoadduprjtdy4wharue6cz7zudid.onion.
* Ransomware notes created by Medusa and Clop.

A malware detection event will be created if a new restore point contains more onion addresses or ransomware notes than the previous restore point selected for comparison. This can trigger a [proactive signature\-based scan](malware_detection_signature_detection.html), if you have it enabled. If both restore points contain the same number of onion addresses or ransomware notes, a malware detection event will not be created. For more details, see [How Inline Scan Works](malware_detection_inline_scan_hiw.html).

| Note |
| --- |
| Inline scan is disabled by default when you install or upgrade to a new version of Veeam Backup \& Replication. If you want to use this functionality, consider the following:* Scanning may increase CPU usage (10\-15% on average) on the backup proxy, depending on the workload type and amount of data. * Scanning may increase RAM usage on the backup server, depending on the amount of data. To analyze 1 million files on a machine, inline scan requires approximately 50 MB RAM. |

Supported Scenarios

When performing backup jobs, you can scan blocks in a data stream from the following machines:

* VMware VMs including VMware Cloud Director VMs
* Hyper\-V VMs
* Nutanix AHV VMs
* Proxmox VE VMs
* Machines with Veeam Agent for Microsoft Windows operating in the managed by backup server mode (volume\-level backup only)
* Microsoft Azure VMs backed up by Veeam Backup for Microsoft Azure

Requirements and Limitations

Inline scan has the following requirements and limitations:

* Scanning is supported only for simple volumes and for the following file systems: NTFS, ext4, ext3, ext2\.
* Scanning dynamic disks and disks encrypted by BitLocker is not supported.
* To store ransomware indexes, you need enough disk space on the backup server. The disk space calculation is based on the following data:

* The number of machines.
* Used disk space per machine.
* The number of restore points per machine.

Per machine, storing ransomware indexes requires approximately 270 KB of disk space on the backup server per 10 GB of used disk space multiplied by the number of restore points.

For example, a machine has 200 GB of used space and 10 restore points. Storing ransomware indexes for this machine requires 54 MB (270 KB \* 20 \* 10 restore points).

* Text artifacts will be detected only if the following conditions are met:

* The block size of the file system is 4 KB.
* The text file has UTF\-8 encoding.
* The text file is not stored in the Master File Table (MFT).

* Detection of "sleeping" malware is not supported.
* Some file types may be unintentionally marked as suspicious during inline scan, for example, Linux packages with LZMA compression, files encrypted with Windows EFS, specific ISO files, and so on. If you have such files, you can mark related malware detection events as false positives. For more information, see [Managing Malware Status](malware_detection_managing_status.html).

In This Section

* [How Inline Scan Works](malware_detection_inline_scan_hiw.html)

Veeam Backup \& Replication supports the following malware detection methods:

**Malware Detection Methods**

| Malware detection method | Scan objects | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| File system activity analysis | Indexing data | When new indexing data appears, detects the following malware activity:* Known suspicious files and extensions * Indicators of compromise * Deleted files * Extension changes  Marks workloads as Suspicious. For more information, see [File System Activity Analysis](malware_detection_guest_index.html). |
| Inline entropy analysis | Blocks in a data stream | For machines, during the backup job, detects the following malware activity:* Encrypted files * Onion links * Ransom notes  Marks workloads as Suspicious. For more information, see [Inline Scan](malware_detection_data_blocks.html). |
| Signature\-based detection (Veeam Threat Hunter) | Restore points | During the Scan Backup session, finds the last clean restore point. For more information, see [Veeam Threat Hunter for Scan Backup](malware_detection_scan_backup_veeam_threat_hunter.html). For machines, during the restore session with the Secure Restore option, detects malware activity. For more information, see [Veeam Threat Hunter for Secure Restore](secure_restore_veeam_threat_hunter.html). During the SureBackup job, detects malware activity. For more information, see [SureBackup Job](surebackup_job.html). Marks workloads as Infected. |
| 3rd party antivirus software | Restore points | During the Scan Backup session, finds the last clean restore point. For more information, see [Antivirus Scan for Scan Backup](malware_detection_scan_backup_antivirus.html). For machines, during the restore session with the Secure Restore option, detects malware activity as specified in the antivirus configuration file. For more information, see [Antivirus Scan for Secure Restore](secure_restore_antivirus.html). During the SureBackup job, detects malware activity. For more information, see [SureBackup Job](surebackup_job.html). Marks workloads as Infected. |
| Rule\-based detection (YARA) | Restore points | During the Scan Backup session, does one of the following:* Finds the last clean restore point * Analyzes the content for specific information  For more information, see [YARA Scan for Scan Backup](malware_detection_scan_backup_yara.html). For machines, during the restore session with the Secure Restore option, detects malware activity as specified in the YARA rule. For more information, see [YARA Scan for Secure Restore](secure_restore_yara.html). During the SureBackup job, detects malware activity. For more information, see [SureBackup Job](surebackup_job.html). Marks workloads as Infected. |
| 3rd party malware protection solution | Depends on the configuration of the malware protection solution | Uses Veeam Incident API to send a request about detected malware activity to Veeam Backup \& Replication. Marks machines as Infected. For more information, see [Veeam Backup \& Replication REST API Reference](https://helpcenter.veeam.com/references/vbr/13/rest/1.3-rev0/tag/Malware-Detection). |

citations.title: Reporting
citations.text:
Reporting
[\#](#reporting)Reporting > [\#](#use-unusual-activities-analysis-report)Use Unusual Activities Analysis Report

Cloud Backup for Salesforce® will learn from your backup activity and warn you of organizations with unusual activities or that are under a potential ransomware attack.

Unusual activities are designed to provide visibility about atypical patterns within your environment, distinct from regular usage patterns. The unusual activities could be related to malware that is related to ransomware or non\-ransomware. But in most cases, they can be legitimate operations. It might be normal for a user to make changes that do not match their day\-to\-day patterns. While you should be aware that these changes are happening, you likely do not have to respond to every unusual activity report.

However, a potential ransomware attack is much more serious and requires your immediate attention. It refers to the real suspicious files that were detected in an organization that requires investigation.

To learn how you use your environment and build the pattern, the **Unusual Activities Analysis** report requires at least 12 days of successful backups. Once any unusual activity or potential ransomware attack has been detected, you will receive an email notification. To enable the alert, refer to [Configure Notifications](/salesforce/configure-settings/configure-notifications.html).

citations.title: Ransomware Detection 101
citations.text:
Ransomware Detection 101
Description > Explaining Ransomware Detection and false\-positives

Datto's Ransomware Detection works by detecting patterns of change in specific file types, rather than analyzing specific files. For example, it's highly unlikely that a user or legitimate program would rapidly and simultaneously: 

* Perform an in\-place file content overwrite with random data.
* Overwrite the content of ONLY the file types that ransomware commonly targets.
* Exclude file types commonly ignored by ransomware.
* Preserve all the original file modified timestamps, including overwritten files.

In a case like this, the Datto device would create an alert for suspected ransomware infection.

Ransomware alerts may sometimes be false\-positives if a legitimate program uncharacteristically updates files. 

If a particular agent persistently false\-alerts for ransomware (with no apparent infection), you can disable detection for that agent from the [Configure Agent Settings](205033354.html) page of the Datto appliance. You should only do this as a last resort.

IMPORTANT  Disabling Ransomware Detection for a protected system will also disable all historical infection reporting for that system until you re\-enable the feature.

Your Datto appliance enables Ransomware Detection by default. You can enable or disable this feature for each protected system individually in the Datto web UI by clicking **Protect \> Configure Agent Settings** (or **Configure System Settings**). You'll see **Ransomware Detection** listed under the **Verification** section.

citations.title: Local Verification
citations.text:
Local Verification 
Advanced Backup Verification: Local Verification > Description > Checks Performed \& Interpreting Results

When enabled, your Datto appliance will run the following validations during the backup process and report the following results:

**Integrity Verification**

* **Filesystem Check:** Checks for critical filesystem errors in the snapshot which could affect its usability. If the snapshot fails the filesystem check, the Datto appliance reports the reason for failure. Filesystem errors typically replicate from the production machine. If you receive a filesystem integrity alert, Datto recommends the following troubleshooting steps:

	1. Run a [Differential Merge](200554185.html) backup, and view the results of the integrity verification.
	2. Run a read\-only chkdsk on the affected server. Address any issues the chkdsk finds. If the chkdsk finds no issues and the local verification still fails, proceed.
	3. Run a `chkdsk /f /r` on the affected server (a server reboot will be required). Address any issues the `chkdsk /f /r` finds.
	4. Run another [Differential Merge](200554185.html) backup.

Further information regarding chkdsk can be found in: [CHKDSK](115005510646.html). 

For Linux system troubleshooting, see [Datto Linux Agent troubleshooting steps](208276503.html). You can also find Linux system troubleshooting information at [linux.org](https://www.linux.org/)*(external link)*.

If you continue to receive failure alerts after performing the above steps, contact [Datto Technical Support](https://www.datto.com/contact).

* **Volume Check**: The Datto appliance will check that the volumes which were captured in the backup match those included for backup in the [Volume\-Level Backup Control](205044014.html) interface. The Datto appliance will alert you if a volume is missing.
* **VSS Check**: This check looks for [VSS writer](200554755.html) failures on the production machine during the backup process, which causes the agent to fall back to the crash\-consistent STC or DBD backup engine to capture a snapshot successfully. This check will only occur if you have configured the agent to [use a fallback engine](200554755.html).

**Ransomware Detection** (Datto Windows Agent only)

* **Ransomware Check:** The Datto appliance will check the snapshot for signs of ransomware, and alert you if an infection is suspected. See the [Ransomware Detection 101](217935123.html) article for more information.

The device GUI reports the results of these checks in the **Local Verified** column of the [Manage Recovery Points](205033104.html) page.  
[

![mceclip1.png](/media/729d0996-7646-4b45-ac4e-5787043f9d80/f9680970bf76.png)

> **Figure:** A legend table showing three icons and their meanings: a green circle indicates successful backup, integrity verification, and ransomware check; an orange circle indicates successful backup but failed integrity or ransomware check; a gray circle indicates a locally deleted recovery point.

](../../Resources/Images/360000946503-803377145.png)

Mousing over the icons in the Datto appliance interface will display a detailed backup report for each snapshot.

citations.title: About Ransomware Detection
citations.text:
About Ransomware Detection
How Eon protects against ransomware > Databases

For databases, Eon examines structured data elements such as tables, rows, schema definitions, and value distributions to identify indicators of ransomware activity or corruption.
Rather than scanning files, Eon analyzes the data itself for these indicators:

* **Row and table count drops**:
Eon detects sudden, unexplained decreases in the number of rows or tables, which can indicate data deletion or destructive encryption.
* **Schema changes**:
Eon identifies unexpected modifications to database schemas, such as dropped or altered tables and columns.
* **Cardinality shifts**:
Eon monitors for unusual changes in value distributions caused by encrypted or overwritten data replacing normal values.
* **Data corruption patterns**:
Eon detects corruption signatures that indicate tampering or bulk data manipulation.
* **Embedded ransomware notes**:
Eon scans for ransom notes inserted into stored datasets, a common tactic where attackers leave demands within the data itself.

Each indicator contributes to a weighted confidence score.
Eon correlates multiple signals before flagging a backup as potentially compromised, reducing false positives while maintaining detection accuracy.

citations.title: About Ransomware Detection
citations.text:
About Ransomware Detection
How Eon handles infected resources

When working with ransomware detection, it’s helpful to understand how ransomware infection status is determined, as well as how Eon handles infected and clean resources.

Infected resources
When Eon finds ransomware indicators on a snapshot, the resource is considered infected.
As long as the latest snapshot contains signs of ransomware, the resource continues to be considered infected.

Eon retains the latest clean snapshot indefinitely, even if its retention period expires.

Ransomware detection typically requires a clean baseline snapshot to compare future snapshots against.
Even so, Eon attempts to identify ransomware indicators on the first snapshot of a new resource.
If ransomware indicators are found, the resource is considered infected from the start.

Clean resources
When the latest snapshot is clean, the resource is considered clean.
This is true even if previous snapshots are infected.

Ransomware notifications
Eon provides notifications for ransomware\-related events, helping you stay informed about the status of your resources and snapshots.
You can enable notifications for these ransomware\-related events:

* Ransomware detected in resource.
* Ransomware detected in snapshot.
* Ransomware infection remediated.
* Resource excluded from ransomware detection.
* Ransomware detection exclusion canceled for resource.

For more information on notifications, see [About Notification Policies](/data-protection/integrations/notifications/about-notification-policies).

Additional information
* [Backup Policy Overview](/data-protection/backup-and-protection/backup-configuration/backup-policies/backup-policy-overview)

citations.title: Threat detection with Microsoft Defender for Cloud (preview)
citations.text:
Overview
Threat detection in Azure Backup with Microsoft Defender for Cloud integration (preview)

Azure Backup integrates with Microsoft Defender for Cloud to offer advanced threat detection for Azure virtual machine (VM) backups. You can use this feature to assess the health of backup restore points by identifying potentially malicious or ransomware\-infected backups.

With security signals from Defender for Servers, Azure Backup detects compromise indicators such as disruption patterns, behavioral anomalies, and ransomware signatures. Defender for Cloud scans the source virtual machine for malware. Azure Backup evaluates the health of restore points by using these signals when it creates the backup snapshot.

Key benefits
Threat detection for Azure VM backups includes the following benefits:

* **Proactive threat identification**: Threat detection configuration at the vault level automatically identifies compromised restore points across all VM backups in the vault. This automatic identification enhances recovery confidence during a ransomware attack.
* **Faster recovery**: The feature can reduce time to recover by quickly identifying clean restore points that are suitable for ransomware recovery.
* **Seamless integration**: The feature works natively with [Defender for Servers Plan 1 and Plan 2](/en-us/azure/defender-for-cloud/defender-for-servers-overview#plan-protection-features) to provide a unified and consistent security experience across Azure workloads.

Source\-scan status for Azure VM backups
You can use the Azure portal to monitor the status of source scans for Azure VM backups. There are two status categories: configuration and summary.

citations.title: Preserve recovery points in response to ransomware alerts
citations.text:
Integrate with Microsoft Defender's ransomware alerts
Integrate Microsoft Defender's ransomware alerts to protect Azure Backup recovery points

This article describes how to integrate Microsoft Defender's ransomware alerts to preserve Azure Backup recovery points. Assume there has been a breach on the Virtual Machine that is protected by both Defender and Azure Backup. Defender detects the ransomware, raises an alert which includes details of the activity and suggested recommendations to remediate. As soon as a ransomware signal is detected from Defender, ensuring backups are preserved (i.e., paused from expiring) to minimize the data loss is top of our customers’ mind.

Azure Backup provides several security capabilities to help you protect your backup data. [Soft delete](backup-azure-security-feature-cloud), [Immutable vaults](backup-azure-immutable-vault-concept), [Multi\-User Authorization (MUA)](multi-user-authorization-concept) are part of a comprehensive data protection strategy for backup data. Soft delete is enabled by default, with option to make it always\-on (irreversible). Soft deleted backup data is retained at no additional cost for *14* days, with option to [extend the duration](backup-azure-enhanced-soft-delete-about). Enabling immutability on vaults can protect backup data by blocking any operations that could lead to loss of recovery points. You can configure Multi\-user authorization (MUA) for Azure Backup as an additional layer of protection to critical operations on your Recovery Services vaults. By default, critical alert for destructive operation (such as stop protection with delete backup data) is raised and an email is sent to subscription owners, admins, and co\-admins.

Microsoft Defender for Cloud (MDC) is a Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) and Cloud Workload Protection Platform (CWPP) for all of your Azure, on\-premises, and multicloud (Amazon AWS and Google GCP) resources. Defender for Cloud generates security alerts when threats are identified in your cloud, hybrid, or on\-premises environment. It's available when you enable enhanced security features. Each alert provides details of affected resources along with the information you need to quickly investigate the issue and steps to take to remediate an attack. If a malware or a ransomware attacks on an Azure Virtual Machine, Microsoft Defender for Cloud detects suspicious activity and indicators associated with ransomware on an Azure VM and generates a Security Alert. Examples of the Defender for Cloud Alerts that trigger on a Ransomware detection: *Ransomware indicators detected*, *Behavior similar to ransomware detected*, and so on.

Note

This solution is scoped to Azure Virtual Machines. You can deploy the logic app only at a subscription level, which means all Azure VMs under the subscription can use the logic app to pause expiry of recovery points in the event of a security alert.

Solution workflow
This solution demonstrates integration of Azure Backup with Microsoft Defender for Cloud (MDC) for detection and response to alerts to accelerate response. The disgram illustrates the following three use cases:

* Ability to send email alerts to the Backup Admin.
* Security Admin to triage and manually trigger logic app to secure backups.
* Workflow to automatically respond to the alert by performing the *Disable Backup Policy (Stop backup and retain data)* operation.

![Diagram shows how Microsoft Defender for Cloud and Azure Backup using Logic apps helps protecting the backup data.](/media/68af57db-6111-49fb-8081-eaeffaad7d59/2180357a18a4.png)

> **Figure:** Diagram illustrating a ransomware protection workflow: an Azure VM is attacked (2), triggering a security alert (3) which activates a Logic app (4). The Logic app stops backups for the affected VM (5), sends an email to the backup admin (5), and after triage (6), backups are resumed via Recovery Services Vault (1).

Prerequisites
* [Enable Azure Backup for Azure virtual machines](tutorial-backup-vm-at-scale).
* [Enable Microsoft Defender for Servers Plan 2 for the Subscription](/en-us/azure/defender-for-cloud/enable-enhanced-security#enable-enhanced-security-features-on-a-subscription).

citations.text:
Using the Anomaly Monitoring dashboard

The Anomaly Monitoring dashboard automatically detects significant changes in your backup data and alerts you when activity falls outside the expected range. This helps you quickly spot issues like accidental deletions, ransomware, or unauthorized changes.

How anomaly detection works
Keepit continuously monitors your backup snapshots and compares each new snapshot against your recent backup history. When the total volume of changes deviates significantly from the norm, the system flags it as an anomaly.

The expected range is calculated from the 60 snapshots preceding the detected anomaly, excluding any snapshots that were themselves anomalous. This gives you a realistic baseline based on your actual backup patterns.

citations.title: VM Encryption Detection
citations.text:
VM Encryption Detection

VM Encryption Detection identifies encryption on the host, allowing you
 to receive anomaly alerts for encryption activity on virtual machines. You can use this
 information to quickly assess the blast radius and recover from such attacks. 

Anomaly Detection in Data Threat Analytics scans data from snapshots to
 detect ransomware attacks that target the file system of the workload object. However,
 when the ESXi host and the associated virtual machine and virtual disk files are
 targeted, snapshots fail due to the attack on the ESXi host. Under these circumstances,
 file systems are compromised. VM Encryption Detection identifies anomalous
 activity on the virtual machine by scanning backup event errors and flags ransomware
 attacks that target the host.

Enabling Data Threat Analytics and Anomaly Detection is required for enabling
 VM Encryption Detection. This feature is available only for vSphere
 virtual machines.

VM Encryption Detection detects multiple types of ransomware attacks,
 including attacks that can bring down the ESXi host completely and attacks that encrypt
 the virtual machine disk (VMDK) extension. In both scenarios, RSC flags
 backup failures in ESXi hosts as anomalies.

You can view anomalies flagged by VM Encryption Detection on the Events page
 in Data Protection. To receive email alerts for any anomalies detected, you can
 configure email notifications in the Settings page. You can recover any affected virtual
 machines from the anomaly details page.

citations.title: Data impact investigation
citations.text:
Data impact investigation

Data impact investigation enables IT and backup administrators to identify the scope
 of objects and files affected by events such as ransomware, mass deletion, or accidental
 data loss, and to recover to a healthy snapshot without switching between tools.

Data impact investigation in Data Threat Analytics enables IT and backup
 administrators to scope and respond to data\-loss events such as ransomware or accidental
 deletion. When an Anomaly Detection alert, Threat Monitoring alert,
 external security tool, or a manual report indicates a suspected mass deletion or
 ransomware event, you can use the Investigation dashboard to identify affected objects,
 examine file change activity across backup snapshots, and initiate recovery, all from a
 single location.

Options for starting an investigation
You can start an investigation from any of three entry points, depending on how the
 problem first surfaces:

* Anomaly Detection or Threat Monitoring alert: RSC flags unusual change patterns in an object's snapshots or
 threat matches, and raises an alert. You can open the flagged object to examine
 its file change activity across a timeline and confirm the scope of the
 event.
* External alert: An external security tool identifies the affected systems. You
 can use the objects and the event timeframe from the alert to scope your search
 on the Investigation dashboard. This is a manual step; there is no automated
 ingestion of alerts from external tools.
* Manual investigation: No alert has fired. You can open the Investigation
 dashboard directly as part of a manual confirmation. For example, when a team
 reports missing files after an accidental deletion, or to validate expected
 changes after a planned operation.

Data impact investigation capabilities
From the Investigation dashboard, you can:

* View all objects with Anomaly Detection enabled and their file change
 activity (added files, modified files, deleted files, and change in object
 size). Change in object size is not reported for Microsoft 365 SharePoint and
 OneDrive objects.
* Filter the object list by platform or object type, and set the time range to
 manage which objects appear in the list.
* Open an individual object view that plots file activity and file extension
 trends across snapshots.
* Access recovery options at the snapshot level or file and folder level.
* Export the file activity for the selected object and time frame as a CSV
 file.

Optional enhancements
The following RSC features add context to investigation results when
 enabled:

* Anomaly detection: Highlights snapshots flagged as anomalous within the
 investigation views.
* Threat hunting and Threat Monitoring: Correlates threat indicators with
 the investigation data. Snapshots that contain quarantined files are flagged in
 the Snapshot tab.
* Sensitive Data Discovery: Adds Hits by Sensitivity and Data Categories
 columns to the File Activity tab and the Browse view, so you can prioritize
 recovery and reporting based on data classification such as financial
 records.

citations.title: Backup scanning plans
citations.text:
Backup scanning plans

To scan backups for malware (including ransomware), create a backup scanning plan.

Backup scanning plans are not supported for all workloads and backup storages. For more details, see [Limitations](antimalware-scan-of-backups.html#Limitations_antimalware_scan).
To create a backup scanning plan

1. In the Cyber Protect console, go to Management \> Backup scanning.
2. In the Actions pane, click Create plan.
3. Change the default plan name.
4. In Backups to scan, click Specify.

	1. \[Optional] To add a new location, click Add, select the location, and then click Done.
	2. Click Locations or Backups to select the scope for the plan.
	3. Select entire location or individual archives in a location.

	You can select one or more items.
	4. Click Done.
5. \[If the selected archives are encrypted] In Encryption, enable the toggle, and then enter the encryption password.

The password you specified will be used for the scanning of all backups in the plan, so all selected archives must use the same encryption password. For archives that use different encryption passwords, create separate plans.
6. Click Create.

As a result, a backup scanning plan is created. The cloud agent will automatically scan the selected archives once an hour. You cannot change the plan schedule or the period between two consecutive scans.

citations.title: Antimalware scan of backups
citations.text:
Antimalware scan of backups

To prevent the recovery of infected files, configure a [backup scanning plan](backup-scanning-plan.html) and ensure that the backups do not contain malware. 

Backup scanning for Microsoft 365 is available only in cloud deployments. You cannot configure a backup scanning plan for Microsoft 365 in an on\-premises deployment.
Antimalware scan of backups is available if the Scan Service component is installed with the Cyber Protect Management Server. For more information, see [Scan Service](scan-service.html). 

Backup scanning plans are supported for Entire machine and Disks/volumes backups of Windows machines. Only volumes with the NTFS file system and GPT or MBR partitioning are scanned.

The following backup storages are supported:

* Cloud storage
* Network folder
* Local folder

Only agents installed on the same workload can access backups in a local folder.

For security and performance reasons, we recommend that you use a dedicated machine for scanning purposes. This machine must have access to all scanned backups.

The backups that you select for scanning can be in one of the following states:

* Not scanned
* No malware
* Malware detected

To check the status, in the Cyber Protect console, go to Backup storage \> Locations, and then check the Status column. The Backup scanning details widget on the Dashboard \> Overview tab also provides information about this status. 

Limitations
* Recovery points with Continuous data protection (CDP) backups are not scanned. Only non\-CDP recovery points of the selected backup set are scanned. For more information about Continuous data protection, see [Continuous data protection (CDP)](continuous-data-protection-acp.html).
* When you perform safe recovery of an Entire machine backup, the data in the CDP recovery point is not automatically recovered. To recover this data, run a Files/folders recovery.
