citations.title: Malware protection
citations.text:
Malware protection
Malware protection in AWS Backup > How to use malware scanning

When you use Amazon GuardDuty Malware Protection with AWS Backup, you can automatically scan your backups for malware. This integration helps you detect malicious code in your backups and identify clean recovery points for restore operations.

Amazon GuardDuty Malware Protection supports two primary workflows for scanning your backups:

* **Automatic malware scanning through backup plans** – Enable malware scanning in backup plans to automate malware detection with AWS Backup. When enabled, AWS Backup automatically initiates an Amazon GuardDuty scan after each successful backup completion. You can configure either full or incremental scanning for specific backup plan rules, which determines how frequently your backups are scanned. For more information about scan types, see [Incremental vs full scans](#malware-scan-types) below. AWS Backup recommends enabling automatic malware scanning in backup plans for proactive threat detection after backup creation.
* **On\-demand scans** – Run on\-demand scans to manually scan existing backups, choosing between full or incremental scan types. AWS Backup recommends using on\-demand scans to identify your last clean backup. When scanning before a restore operation, use a full scan to examine the entire backup with the latest threat detection model.

citations.title: Malware protection
citations.text:
Malware protection
Malware protection in AWS Backup > Incremental vs full scans

With malware scanning, you have the option to choose between incremental and full scans based on your security requirements and cost considerations.

**Incremental scans** analyze only the data that changed between the target and base recovery point. These scans are faster and more cost\-effective for regular scanning, making them ideal for frequent periodic backups where you want to scan newly backed up data.

Even when incremental scanning is selected, AWS Backup performs a full scan in these situations:

* **First\-time scans:** The initial scan of a resource is always a full scan, allowing Amazon GuardDuty to establish a baseline of potential threats. Subsequent scans will then be incremental.
* **Expired baseline:** If your baseline recovery point was scanned more than 365 days ago, a full scan occurs. Because Amazon GuardDuty retains finding information for only 365 days, a new baseline must be established to ensure accurate scanning results.
* **Deleted baseline:** If your base recovery point is deleted before your next incremental scan starts, a full scan occurs automatically.

**Full scans** examine the entire recovery point regardless of previous scans. While these scans provide comprehensive coverage, they take longer to complete and incur higher costs. You can run full scans on\-demand or schedule them through your backup plans. AWS Backup recommends configuring periodic full scans in your backup plans at extended intervals to ensure your entire backup data is regularly scanned with the latest malware signature model.

For optimal security versus cost management, consider your backup frequency when choosing scan types. When you configure malware scanning for Amazon S3 continuous backups, your scan job will run at the frequency of the corresponding backup rule.

Note
 On\-demand scans for Amazon S3 continuous backups do not support incremental scans. Instead you can scan up to any restorable point in time. 

Note
Incremental malware scanning is not supported for Amazon EC2 recovery points in a [logically air\-gapped vault](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-backup/latest/devguide/logicallyairgappedvault.html) or copied Amazon EC2 recovery points. 

Note
AWS Backup does not support using a recovery point scanned only via on\-demand scan from Amazon GuardDuty as a base recovery point for incremental scans. To perform incremental scans via AWS Backup, ensure AWS Backup has previously scanned the base recovery point.

citations.title: Use Cases
citations.text:
Use Cases

Overview[](https://docs.trilio.io/kubernetes/overview/use-cases#overview)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------

Backup and recovery capabilities within Trilio for Kubernetes enable a plethora of use cases and opportunities for customers. An explanation of two metrics are particularly important when building use cases around application resiliency: RPO and RTO

Recovery Point Objective[](https://docs.trilio.io/kubernetes/overview/use-cases#recovery-point-objective)
Recovery Point Objective (RPO) determines data lag of backup images with respect to the latest production data.

Recovery Time Objective[](https://docs.trilio.io/kubernetes/overview/use-cases#recovery-time-objective)
Recovery Time Objective (RTO) determines how long it takes to recover an application from backup data.

Trilio supports Backup/Snapshot policies that helps you implement your application specific RPOs. You can schedule a Backup/Snapshot as frequently as 1 hr to implement a better RPO for your applications.

Data Protection[](https://docs.trilio.io/kubernetes/overview/use-cases#data-protection)
Based on Trilio's backup and recovery technology, point-in-time backups/snapshots and restores can be created for cloud-native applications protecting them from data corruption or other malicious activity on production data.

Ransomware claimed nearly ~$40K in Q3 2019, and organizations had data unavailable for an average of 12.1 days amongst other direct and indirect losses. Point-in-time data protection is a key solution to help protect data from Ransomware outages.

Disaster Recovery[](https://docs.trilio.io/kubernetes/overview/use-cases#disaster-recovery)
Based on Trilio's backup and recovery technology, point-in-time Backups/Snapshots and restores can be created for cloud-native applications protecting them from data corruption or other malicious activity on production data.

The same backup and recovery technology can be leveraged in case of outages at the primary site to restore an entire environment to a separate location, fulfilling Disaster Recovery.

Trilio Backups/Snapshots are application aware and includes all artifacts that define the application. These include persistent data, Pod definitions, config maps, secrets, and other items. It recovers the entire application allowing you to achieve the most optimal RTO possible.

Migration[](https://docs.trilio.io/kubernetes/overview/use-cases#migration)
You may need to migrate applications from one cloud platform to another or one Kubernetes cluster to a different Kubernetes cluster. Most businesses and compliance initiatives are now mandating IT organizations to have a proven multi-cloud strategy - so that \*\*\*\* they are not locked to a specific cloud vendor. IT departments are now required to demonstrate their multi-cloud strategy by recovering business applications in multiple clouds. By choosing cloud storage as backup/snapshot target, Trilio can demonstrate an application migration use case.

Test and Development[](https://docs.trilio.io/kubernetes/overview/use-cases#test-and-development)
Another popular use case is test and development for DevOps. There are a plethora of tools that can help you achieve DevOps, but most of them lack the capability to version control the production data. Exiting DevOp tools can help version control the code and help you streamline processes. However, in some instances you may a need point-in-time of production data for you DevOps processes including identifying performance bottlenecks, troubleshooting data corruption and other issues. Trilio can reliably restore a point-in-time of your production application including its associated data for test and development needs.

Ransomware Protection[](https://docs.trilio.io/kubernetes/overview/use-cases#ransomware-protection)
Trilio provides and will continue to innovate its strategy to protect against ransomware attacks. Ransomware protection from Trilio is aligned to the pillars of the NIST and NCCoE cybersecurity frameworks. The pillars are defined as Identify and Protect, Detect and Mitigate, and Recover. Trilio has built (and is building) features to align with these pillars:

1.  Identify and Protect - Application discovery, Security Validations Immutable backups/snapshots, Encryption, Zero-Trust etc.

2.  Detect and Mitigate - Scanning of Backups/snapshots, Anomaly Detection, Notifications into Slack/Teams etc.

3.  Recover - Deep logging, Isolation testing, DR workflows and multiple target types to increase recoverability surface.

citations.title: Encryption Detection
citations.text:
Encryption Detection

Note: Encryption Detection is only supported on VMware.
Zerto 's Encryption Analyzer uses real\-time inspection of protected VMs' writes to identify anomalous encryption activity.

When higher or irregular amounts of encrypted traffic are detected, Zerto issues an alert ([ENC0001](https://help.zerto.com/bundle/Alarms.Alerts.HTML/page/ENC0001.htm)) so you can assess whether the anomalies are expected behavior or could be indicators of compromise from malware.

Zerto automatically tags checkpoints in the Zerto journal to help identify which recovery points were created before the anomaly and which came after.

The feature is **enabled** by default.

* **[How Encryption Detection Works](https://help-be.zerto.com/bundle/Admin.VC.HTML.10.9/page/How_Encryption_Detection_Works.htm)**
* **[Encryption Detection Checkpoints](https://help-be.zerto.com/bundle/Admin.VC.HTML.10.9/page/Encryption_Detection_Checkpoints.htm)**
* **[Enabling and Disabling Encryption Detection in the User Interface](https://help-be.zerto.com/bundle/Admin.VC.HTML.10.9/page/Enabling_Disabling_Encryption_Detection_UI.htm)**
* **[Enabling and Disabling Encryption Detection in the API](https://help-be.zerto.com/bundle/Admin.VC.HTML.10.9/page/Enabling_Disabling_Encryption_Detection_API.htm)**
* **[Dismissing the Encryption Detection Alert](https://help-be.zerto.com/bundle/Admin.VC.HTML.10.9/page/Dismissing_Encryption_Detection_Alert.htm)**

citations.title: How Encryption Detection Works
citations.text:
How Encryption Detection Works

Zerto's encryption detection feature uses a suspicion level indicator to classify potential abnormal encryption behaviors. The suspicion level is graded on a scale:

* 1: low suspicion

At this level, two tagged checkpoints are created automatically. See [Encryption Detection Checkpoints](https://help-be.zerto.com/bundle/Admin.VC.HTML.10.9/page/Encryption_Detection_Checkpoints.htm) .
* 2: high suspicion

At this level, Zerto performs the following actions:

	+ Two tagged checkpoints are created automatically. See [Encryption Detection Checkpoints](https://help-be.zerto.com/bundle/Admin.VC.HTML.10.9/page/Encryption_Detection_Checkpoints.htm) .
	+ The [ENC0001](https://help.zerto.com/bundle/Alarms.Alerts.HTML/page/ENC0001.htm) alert is triggered.
	+ The status of the affected
	 VPG (s) becomes Warning: potential abnormal encryption was detected. The
	 alert contains information about the volume(s), VM(s) and VPG(s) that
	 are affected.

![](/media/307c98fb-bf69-4d69-a94c-dc7072b9e139/2c8c0c7570ac2b25.png)

> **Figure:** Screenshot of the Monitoring screen showing one active alert (ENC0001) for abnormal encryption behavior around a VPG: File Server, affecting virtual machine FileServer01 and volume nfs-left-prod01. The alert description is expanded in a tooltip.

The suspicion levels are displayed via APIs. See [Encryption Detection APIs](https://help-be.zerto.com/bundle/Admin.VC.HTML.10.9/page/Encryption_Detection_APIs.htm) .

After investigating the event, you can either start recovery (see [Managing Failover](https://help-be.zerto.com/bundle/Admin.VC.HTML.10.9/page/Managing_Failover.htm) ) or dismiss the event (see [Dismissing the Encryption Detection Event](https://help-be.zerto.com/bundle/Admin.VC.HTML.10.9/page/Dismissing_Encryption_Detection_Alert.htm) )

**Parent topic:** [Encryption Detection](https://help-be.zerto.com/bundle/Admin.VC.HTML.10.9/page/Encryption_Detection.htm)

citations.title: Creating a custom policy
citations.text:
Creating a custom policy
3 Establishing a data protection environment > Creating an R-Shield policy

You can create an R-Shield policy that helps ensure integrity and security of your data. When configuring the R-Shield policy, you can enable the following:

- l Anomaly detection to check the backup data size and detect changes in the standard deviation of the data size between backups. The result is the anomaly detection status.
- l Malware scanning to scan backed-up data for threats that are recognizable by using the YARA rules. The result is the malware detection status.

Anomaly detection and malware scanning begin after the R-Shield option is enabled in a policy and that policy is assigned to an entity. For instructions, see 'Creating a policy' on page 134.

After you create an R-Shield policy and enable the R-Shield option in a policy that is assigned to an entity, you can do the following:

- l View the R-Shield status for the entities to which this policy is assigned. The R-Shield status is visible in the R-Shield column in the relevant panels and in the Detail view for all the available restore points. By hovering over the RShield icon, if enabled, you can also separately see the anomaly detection

- and malware detection statuses. For details about the R-Shield statuses, see 'Viewing entity details' on page 399.
- l Run malware scans manually. For details, see 'Running malware scans manually' on page 431.

Prerequisites
Only if you plan to enable malware scanning.

- l For virtual machines, applications, and volume groups: You must own a premium tier Platform license. For details, see 'Licensing' on page 488.
- l For file shares: A HYCU instance is required. For details, see 'HYCU instances' on page 25.

Limitations
Only if you plan to enable malware scanning. Malware scanning is not supported for the following entities:

- l Volume groups that are not attached to virtual machines. Malware scanning can be run only for an entire virtual machine and the attached volume groups.
- l Generic file shares.
- l Buckets.

Considerations
- l If you delete an R-Shield policy, the R-Shield option is automatically disabled in the policies that use the deleted R-Shield policy.
- l If after enabling malware scanning you notice an increasing number of queued malware scan jobs in the Jobs panel, the available resources for malware scanning are insufficient. To make more resources available, you can do the following:
- o Follow the recommended system requirements for your HYCU backup controller. For details, see 'Sizing resources for your HYCU backup infrastructure' on page 27.
- o Increase the available memory on your HYCU instance. To do so, sign in to the management console of the environment where the HYCU instance is deployed, and then modify the memory configuration as required.
- o Deploy additional HYCU instances in your data protection environment.

- For instructions, see 'Creating a HYCU instance by using the HYCU web user interface' on page 484
- l For malware scanning: The YARA rules that are used for malware scanning are automatically updated from the public ReversingLabs repository.

Recommendation
Only if you plan to enable malware scanning. For optimal malware scanning performance, the following is recommended:

- l A HYCU instance should be available in your data protection environment. If a HYCU instance is not available, malware scanning is performed by the HYCU backup controller. Running malware scans on the HYCU backup controller may have a significant impact on its resources and could cause delays in data protection tasks.
- l To perform malware scanning with maximum speed, enable hardwareassisted virtualization on the HYCU instance (if available) or the HYCU backup controller.

citations.title: Running malware scans manually
citations.text:
Running malware scans manually
Running malware scans manually

HYCU runs malware scans automatically after you create an R-Shield policy with enabled malware scanning and enable the R-Shield option in a policy that is assigned to an entity. However, you can at any time decide to manually run a malware scan of all files in the backup or only of the files that change between the selected restore point and the last successful backup. For example, this is useful if you want to run a malware scan for a specific restore point or if a malware scan job fails.

Prerequisites
- l You must have the Administrator user role assigned.
- l The R-Shield option must be enabled in the policy that is assigned to the entity and malware scanning must be enabled in the corresponding R-Shield policy. For details, see 'Creating an R-Shield policy' on page 148.
- l Only if you plan to run malware scanning for file shares:
- o The selected restore point must contain the Snapshot tier.
- o A HYCU instance is required. For details, see 'HYCU instances' on page 25.

Limitations
- l You can run malware scanning for one restore point at a time.
- l If any malware scans or restore jobs are already in progress for the selected restore point, you cannot manually run a malware scan.
- l For file shares: If the selected restore point contains a full backup, you can only scan all files.
- l For the volume groups that are not attached to a virtual machine, for generic file shares, and for buckets: Malware scanning is not supported.

Depending on the type of data that you want to scan for malware, access one of the following panels:

- l Accessing the Applications panel To access the Applications panel, in the navigation pane, click Applications .
- l Accessing the Virtual Machines panel

To access the Virtual Machines panel, in the navigation pane, click Virtual Machines .

- l Accessing the Shares panel To access the Shares panel, in the navigation pane, click Shares .
- l Accessing the Volume Groups panel To access the Volume Groups panel, in the navigation pane, click Volume Groups .

Procedure
1. In the relevant panel, click the entity whose data you want to scan for malware.
2. In the Detail view that appears at the bottom of the screen, select the preferred restore point.

Note The Detail view appears only if you click an entity. Selecting the check box before the name of the entity will not open the Detail

-  view.
3. Click the icon, and then click Run Malware Scan .
4. From the Scan From drop-down menu, select which tier you want to use for the scan. Your restore point can contain one or more tiers among which you can select:
- l Archive
- l Backup
- l Copy
- l Snapshot
5. Depending on the preferred scope of scan, do one of the following:
- l Select Scan all files to scan all of the files that the selected restore point contains.
- l Select Scan changed files to scan the files that have been created or modified since the last successful backup.
6. Click Run .

citations.title: Add an Assured Security - Malware Scan Task to a Policy
citations.text:
Add an Assured Security - Malware Scan Task to a Policy
Add an Assured Security \- Malware Scan Task to a Policy

The Assured Security \- Malware Scan allows you to scan the backup or copy data in recovery points for any malware or malicious files. This feature also warns you about the malicious files in recovery points before restoring. You can run the Assured Security \- Malware Scan manually or according to the specified schedule.

**Notes:** 

* The Assured Security \- Malware Scan is supported only for Windows sources.
* When EFS is enabled on the backed up data on source, and you are using the remote Assured Security proxy, the Assured Security \- Malware Scan job cannot detect the malicious content as the data encrypted with EFS cannot be decrypted into another machine.
* If the files or folders are password protected, the Assured Security \- Malware Scan job cannot detect the malicious content.

You can run the Assured Security \- Malware Scan for the following backup tasks:

* Agent\-based Windows Backup
* Agentless VM Backup to RPS
* Copy from remotely\-managed RPS
* UNC/NFS Backup to RPS
* Oracle Database Backup to RPS

This section contains the following topics:

citations.title: Configuring malware scan for virtual machine backup sets before restore
citations.text:
Configuring malware scan for virtual machine backup sets before restore

 Malware Detection feature provides the ability to perform a scan on virtual machine backup sets. Malware scan operation can be run as an ad hoc job on a given backup set or it can be run as part of the restore operation.

 You can use the feature for the following scenarios:

* To ensure a malware free backup image before a restore operation for business continuity.
* To perform a scan before sending a copy of the backup set to a secondary storage.
* To scan specific backups of interest for compliance purposes, recovery readiness, or any other reason.

 The scan can be run on VMware and Hyper\-V virtual machines and only supports GRT enabled backup sets for disk and deduplication disk devices.

 All the previous backup sets in the backup chain of the selected set should be GRT enabled backup sets on supported devices.

 Backup Exec now supports Symantec Protection Engine (SPE) that can be used for malware scan. The malware scan settings dialog now provides the option to select the scan engine that can be used to perform malware scan. You can choose either Microsoft Windows Defender or SPE. By default, Backup Exec uses Windows Defender to run the malware scan on the backup set chain. Ensure that you have enabled Microsoft Defender and have the updated antivirus definitions. Backup Exec depends on the output of Windows Defender to determine if a backup set is malware free. Ensure that you have valid license for the SPE and the SPE services are running when you choose SPE for malware scan. Backup Exec depends on the output of the SPE to determine if a backup set is malware free.

 For an incremental backup, the previous backup sets in the recovery chain are also used for the scan, but only the selected incremental set is marked as scanned.

 To perform a malware scan, the selected backup set and previous sets in its backup chain are mounted. Each volume of the virtual machine from the mounted backup set is scanned for malware using the scan engine that is selected on the Malware scan settings.

 You can choose to run malware scan as part of the physical virtual machine restore or GRT restore operation. If you perform a GRT restore, the entire virtual machine backup is scanned before performing the restore.

 Backup Exec lets you modify the settings of the malware scan job. Scanning a backup set is CPU intensive and can take significant time if the virtual machine backup has large data to scan. This increases the time taken by the restore job and should be scheduled accordingly. It may affect other applications if you run multiple scan jobs. Go to Backup Exec Settings \> Malware Scan to update the settings.

 Malware scan is only supported for Backup Exec media server with Windows 2016 or later. Malware scan jobs can be run on an ad hoc basis by selecting the VMware and Hyper\-V virtual machine backup sets. An ad hoc malware scan job cannot be run for GRT sets of a virtual machine.

 Malware scan status for virtual machines

 To see the malware scan status, on the Backup and Restore tab or the Storage tab, double\-click the server or the storage device that is related to the backup sets that you want to view and then click Backup Sets.

 For the selected server or storage view, the Malware Scan Status and Malware Scan Time fields are displayed.

 The scan time is the time when malware scan was last run on that set.

 The scan operation displays the following malware status for the virtual machine backup set:

* Malware found

 Indicates that malware is found in one or more volumes that are mounted from the backup set.

* Malware not found

 Indicates no malware being found in the scan of all the volumes of the backup set.

 Best practices for using malware scan

 Note the following best practices for using malware scan:

* It is recommended to run only one malware scan job at a time.
* It is recommended to schedule a malware scan job outside the backup window.
* It is recommended to not have any other antivirus on Backup Exec if Windows Defender is enabled for malware scan.
* It is recommended to not have any other antivirus on Backup Exec if Symantec Protection Engine (SPE) is used for malware scan.
* It is recommended to turn off the Real\-Time of Microsoft Windows Defender, if you are using SPE for malware scan.
* It is recommended to have the valid license and SPE services running when you are using the SPE for malware scan.
* It is recommended to keep Windows Defender virus definitions updated on the Backup Exec server when malware scan is used.
* It is recommended to use default values in job and configuration sets while running the scan job.

Security
Multi-server configuration[](https://documentation.atempo.com/lina-7.4/lina-7.4-en/administration-guide/settings/security#multi-server-configuration)

In this configuration, you:

*   Must enter a line that specifies the name or address of the corporate network gateway and the name or address of the Lina master server on the corporate network.

The syntax to use for each network gateway is: <corporate\_gateway\_name\_ or \_ adress>=<private\_aln\_master\_server\_name\_or\_adress>

For example: gateway=alnserver or 192.168.1.254=192.168.1.42

*   Can also enter a line to manage node access. The syntax to use for each node is:

<corporate\_gateway\_name\_or\_adress>|<node\_name\_or\_address>=<private\_aln\_ node\_name\_or\_address>

Detecting unusual or suspicious backup activity[](https://documentation.atempo.com/lina-7.4/lina-7.4-en/administration-guide/settings/security#detecting-unusual-or-suspicious-backup-activity)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

You can detect unusual or suspicious backup activity on your agents:

*   Unusual activity can be detected when an unusual amount of protected volume is sent from an agent to the server.

*   Suspicious activity can be detected when an agent's compression rate undergoes a sudden change (for example, in the event of a cryptovirus attack). The compression rate is the ratio of the number of blocks calculated over the chosen time period used to compile the average activity.

*   Suspicious activity detection can be enabled for all tenants at once at the server level by a superadministrator, or by an administrator for a specific tenant, with settings inherited from the server if no configuration is defined at the tenant level.

You can sort agents with suspicious or unusual activity using the **Alerts** filter in the agent list. An agent with unusual or suspicious activity can still be backed up.

**To detect unusual or suspicious backup activity:**

1.  Select the tenant(s) for which you want to enable detection.

2.  Go to **Settings > Security > Backup Activity**.

3.  Enable the **Monitor backup activity** option.

4.  Set the settings used to analyze backup activity:

    1.  Set a frequency for the recurring analysis. This analysis can be set in hours, days, weeks, or months.

    2.  Select a time period over which the average activity is compiled. This period can be set in days, weeks, or months.

5.  Set the detection settings for triggering alerts:

    1.  Set one or more thresholds for a specific number of modified files or added blocks, or for the volume transferred by the agent.

    2.  Enable alerts for unusual and suspicious activity, then set a value for each alert type. The server only triggers an alert once one or more thresholds and the value defined for an alert type are reached.

6.  (Optional) Click **Test this configuration** to check whether an agent meets all the criteria you have defined. Testing your configuration does not generate an alarm.

7.  Click **Apply this configuration**.

citations.title: Backup History report
citations.text:
Backup History report

The Backup History report contains backup results of all protected and unprotected assets within the selected date range for the selected appliance(s).

After generating the report, you can view the details of a specific job by clicking it in the grid. This opens the Backup Status: Report Entry dialog. For file\-level backups, you can click Details in this dialog to view and/or export a list of files contained in the backup.

When finished, click Report Categories in the upper left to return to the Available Reports page.

[![Closed](https://help.unitrends.kaseya.com/help/Skins/Default/Stylesheets/Images/transparent.gif)Report details](#)

An example report is given here. Refer to the table below for a description of the available report columns. Not all columns display by default. To customize your output, click the [![Column chooser Icon](/media/2dfd1497-232e-4df7-b66b-cf161734946e/a605759a46fcb01c.png)](../Resources/Images/Reports/column-chooser-icon.png) icon to the right of the column header.

[

![Backup Hist report](/media/2dfd1497-232e-4df7-b66b-cf161734946e/ab3759a89d0ce4a8.png)

> **Figure:** Screenshot of the Backup History report screen showing a table of backup jobs with columns for Protected Asset, Start Date, End Date, Elapsed Time, Job Name, Status, Size (GB), Appliance Name, Type, ID, and At Risk. The image includes callouts explaining how to resize columns, sort by clicking arrows, filter by entering text, and export data as PDF or CSV.

](../Resources/Images/Reports/backup-hist-rpt.png)

| Report Field | Field Description |
| --- | --- |
| App Name | Application type: ●   For host\-level backups, contains the virtual host type. Examples: VMware, XenServer, Hyper\-V 2012 R2\. ●   For application backups, contains the application type. Examples: SQL Server 2012, Oracle 11, Exchange 2013\. ●   For agent\-based backups, contains Image Level or is empty for file\-level.  ●   For System Metadata contains system information, such as appliance configuration and settings. System Metadata is copied to the target during backup copy jobs if changes to this system information are detected. |
| Protected Asset | The name of the asset. |
| Complete | Indicates whether the job completed: True (yes) or False (no). |
| Database Name | For application backups, contains the name of the protected database. For host\-level backups, contains the name of the protected virtual machine. |
| Encrypted | Indicates whether the backup is encrypted: True (yes) or False (no). |
| Start Date | The date and time at which the backup job started. |
| End Date | The date and time at which the backup job completed. |
| Elapsed Time | The amount of time it took for the job to complete, in *hh*:*mm*:*ss* format. |
| Files | For file\-level backups, indicates the number of files in the backup. |
| Instance Name | For application backups, contains the database instance name. For host\-level backups, contains one of the following:  ●   The name of the virtual machine. ●   The name of the ESXi host if that host is being managed by a vCenter. |
| Job Name | Name of the backup job. Job No Longer Exists displays if this backup is no longer stored on the appliance. |
| Copy Status | Status that indicates whether the backup has been copied to the Unitrends Cloud or copied to another Unitrends appliance:  ●   Completed \- The backup copy job is complete. ●   Needed \- Cannot determine the status of this backup's copy job. ●   In progress \- The backup copy job is currently running. ●   Waiting \- The backup copy job is queued but has not yet started. ●   N/A \- This asset's backups are not configured for hot backup copy. |
| Size (GB) | The size of the backup, in gigabytes. |
| Status | Status of the backup job: Success, Warning, or Failure. |
| Appliance Name | The name of the backup appliance. |
| Type | Backup mode: Full, Incremental, Differential, Synthetic Full, Selective, Bare Metal, or Transaction (SQL only). |
| Certify Status | Indicates whether this Recovery Point has been certified by Copy Data Management or by the Unitrends ReliableDR product: Success (has been certified), Failure (has not been certified), or None (this job is not configured for certification). |
| ID | The system\-generated job ID. |
| Verify Status | Indicates whether the appliance verified the backup and the verification status: Success (verified), Failure (verify failed), or N/A (this job is not configured to verify the backup). |
| Speed (MB/S) | Average transfer rate of the job, in megabytes per second. |
| At Risk | Indicates if a potential ransomware infection was discovered: True (potentially infected) or False (not infected). |
